headline: Holgate's New Cut Holds Bait — Fluke Sliding to the Inlets as the Bay Cooks Off
subhead: The back bay is warm and soft, the ocean side is starting to whisper albie, and the real question this week is which cut holds the bait when the tide turns.
body_markdown:
Flew a drone over the Holgate cut this week just to see what the last few blows did to the sandbar, and the read is worth passing along before we get into the bite. The outer bar off the Rip has slid north maybe forty yards since mid-August, and there's a new gut forming on the inside edge that's throwing a rip current visible from three hundred feet up. That kind of structure change matters right now because everything in this zone — fluke, blues, the first albie scouts — is keying on where current concentrates bait, and that cut is doing exactly that on the back half of the outgoing.

The bigger picture for LBI and Great Bay this week is a classic late-August hangover. Water in the back bay has stayed warm and soft, which is why the fluke bite has thinned out the way we said it would — this is the seasonal slide, not a collapse, and it's pushing fish toward the inlets and ocean-front structure where there's cooler, better-oxygenated water moving. We flagged this pattern last week, said the fluke bite would stay soft through the weekend until a real cool-down hits in September, and that's exactly what's playing out. Nothing dramatic, just a slow bleed of fish off the flats and into the current lines.

Fluke are still catchable, just work-for-it catchable. Best results are coming on white Gulp Swimming Mullets paired with 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel edges at Barnegat Light Inlet and the deeper water off the Ship Bottom jetties. Little Egg Inlet is holding fish too, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb when the current funnels bait out of Graveling Point and the Mullica flats and stacks it against the inlet's south edge. Depth there runs 15 to 20 feet with a hard sand bottom — keep the bucktail ticking, don't rip it, and expect keepers mixed with a lot of shorts.

Back in Great Bay and up the Mullica, the summer pattern is still humming — croaker, spot, and spike weakfish on live minnows fished on the bottom near Graveling Point and the deeper holes off Mott Creek. It's a soft bite, but it's a real one, and it's the kind of thing that keeps rods bent for kids and visiting anglers while the bigger fish sort themselves out elsewhere. That pattern typically holds into early September before the water starts to turn.

Bluefish remain the most dependable predator in the zone right now, and that's tracking exactly with what the bait is doing. Bunker schools are still showing along the ocean side beaches from Barnegat Light down through Beach Haven, and where the bunker balls up tight, the blues are all over them — chunking bunker off the beach at first light, or working diamond jigs and metal-lip swimmers through the pods when they're visible from the sand. Expect this to hold through Labor Day week as long as the bunker stay put, and there's no sign yet of them thinning out.

Stripers are still in a holding pattern here, which matches what's happening up and down the coast. There are fish around — some being picked off structure at the inlet mouths on bucktails and swim shads during the last of the outgoing — but the real fall push hasn't started. The trigger is bait density, and with the moon building toward full over the next week, tidal flow is going to increase and start concentrating bunker in the key zones. When that bunker gets thick enough in Little Egg and along the ocean beaches, that's when the bass start committing in numbers instead of picking at scraps. Watch for that shift to start showing in the next week to ten days, not this week.

The wildcard worth rigging for right now is albies and bonito. Both species are already active to the north and south of this stretch, and with warm water still sitting on the ocean side and bait pushed up tight against the inlets, there's a real chance they show inside Barnegat Light's rip or off the end of Holgate within the next several days. Keep a bag ready for a quick switch — small metal like a half-ounce Deadly Dick or a Game Changer epoxy jig, light spinning gear, no wire. If the birds start working tight over bait balls off the Rip or the south end of the island, that's the tell.

Looking at the next few days, expect continuity more than change. The fluke bite stays soft and inlet-focused, bluefish keep pace with the bunker, and the back bay minnow bite holds for Great Bay and the Mullica. The bigger story to watch is the moon building toward full — that's going to push more water through the cuts, sharpen the current lines, and set the stage for the first real signs of the fall transition. If there's only one window worth prioritizing this week, it's the last two hours of the outgoing at Little Egg Inlet or Barnegat Light, right where the new structure is funneling bait. That's where the next move in this zone is going to show up first.
